title: Part 6, Chapter 5
paragraphs: Raskolnikov walked after him.
“What's this?” cried Svidrigailov, turning around. “I thought I said—”
“It means I'm not going to lose sight of you now.”
“What?”
They both stood still and stared at one another, as if measuring each other's strength.

“From all your half-drunk stories,” Raskolnikov observed harshly, “I am absolutely positive that you haven't given up your designs on my sister — you're pursuing them more actively than ever. I've learned that my sister received a letter this morning. You've hardly been able to sit still all this time… You may have dug up a wife along the way, but that means nothing. I'd like to make certain for myself.”
Raskolnikov could hardly have said himself what he wanted or what he wished to make certain of.
“Good heavens! I'll call the police!”
“Go ahead and call them!”

Again they stood for a minute facing each other. At last Svidrigailov's face shifted. Having satisfied himself that Raskolnikov wasn't frightened by his threat, he put on a cheerful, friendly expression.

“What a fellow you are! I deliberately held back from mentioning your affair, though I'm eaten up with curiosity. It's a fantastic business. I had put it off for another time, but you're enough to wake the dead… Well, let's go, but I warn you in advance — I'm only going home for a moment to get some money, then I'll lock up the flat, take a cab, and go spend the evening at the Islands. Now really, are you going to follow me?”
“I'm coming to your lodgings, but not to see you — to see Sofya Semyonovna, to tell her I'm sorry I wasn't at the funeral.”

“Suit yourself, but Sofya Semyonovna isn't at home. She's taken the three children to an elderly lady of high rank, a patroness of some orphan asylums whom I used to know years ago. I charmed the old lady by depositing a sum of money with her to provide for the three children of Katerina Ivanovna, and by subscribing to the institution as well. I also told her Sofya Semyonovna's story in full detail, suppressing nothing. It had an indescribable effect on her. That's why Sofya Semyonovna has been invited to call today at the X. Hotel, where the lady is currently staying.”
“No matter — I'll come all the same.”

“As you please, it makes no difference to me. But I won't come with you. Here we are, we're home. By the way, I'm convinced you regard me with suspicion precisely because I've shown such restraint and haven't troubled you with questions so far… you follow me? It struck you as extraordinary — I'd bet on it. Well, that's what you get for being delicate!”
“And for listening at doors!”

“Ah, so that's it?” Svidrigailov laughed. “Yes, I'd have been surprised if you'd let that slide after everything that's happened. Ha-ha! Though I did grasp something of the pranks you were up to and were telling Sofya Semyonovna about, what was the meaning of it all? Maybe I'm hopelessly behind the times and can't understand. For goodness' sake, explain it to me, my dear boy. Expound the latest theories!”
“You couldn't have heard anything. You're making it all up!”

“But I'm not talking about that (though I did hear something). No, I'm talking about the way you keep sighing and groaning now. The Schiller in you rises up in revolt every other minute, and now you tell me not to listen at doors. If that's how you feel, go inform the police that you had this misfortune — that you made a little mistake in your theory. But if you're convinced that one mustn't listen at doors, yet one may murder old women at one's pleasure, you'd better clear off to America, and quickly too. Run, young man! There may still be time. I mean it sincerely. Are you short of cash? I'll pay your fare.”
“I'm not thinking about any of that,” Raskolnikov interrupted with disgust.

“I understand (but don't put yourself out, don't discuss it if you'd rather not). I understand the questions tormenting you — moral ones, yes? Duties of citizen and man? Set them all aside. They're nothing to you now, ha-ha! You'll say you're still a man and a citizen. If so, you shouldn't have gotten tangled up in this. It's no use taking on a job you're not cut out for. Well — you'd better shoot yourself, or don't you want to?”
“You seem to be trying to enrage me, to make me leave you.”

“What a strange fellow you are! Well, here we are. Welcome to the staircase. You see, that's the way up to Sofya Semyonovna. Look, there's no one home. Don't you believe me? Ask Kapernaumov. She leaves the key with him. Here's Madame Kapernaumov herself. Hey — what? She's rather deaf. Has she gone out? Where? Did you hear that? She's not in and won't be back until late in the evening, probably. Well, come to my room — you wanted to come and see me, didn't you? Here we are. Madame Resslich is out. She's a woman who's always busy, an excellent woman, I assure you… She might have been of use to you if you'd been a little more sensible. Now, look: I take this five-percent bond out of the bureau — see what a pile of them I still have — this one will be turned into cash today. I mustn't waste any more time. The bureau is locked, the flat is locked, and here we are again on the stairs. Shall we take a cab? I'm going to the Islands. Would you like a lift? I'll take this carriage. Ah, you refuse? You've had enough of it! Come for a drive! I think it's going to rain. Never mind, we'll put the hood down…”

Svidrigailov was already in the carriage. Raskolnikov decided that his suspicions were, at least for that moment, unjust. Without answering a word, he turned and walked back toward the Hay Market. If he had only looked back on his way, he might have seen Svidrigailov get out less than a hundred paces off, dismiss the cab, and set off on foot along the pavement. But he had already turned the corner and could see nothing. Intense disgust drew him away from Svidrigailov.
“To think that I could for a single instant have looked for help from that coarse brute, that depraved sensualist and scoundrel!” he cried.

Raskolnikov's judgment had been delivered too lightly and too hastily: there was something about Svidrigailov that lent him a certain original, even mysterious, character. As far as his sister was concerned, Raskolnikov was convinced that Svidrigailov would not leave her in peace. But it was too tiresome and unbearable to keep thinking and thinking about it.

Once alone, he hadn't gone twenty paces before he sank, as usual, into deep thought. On the bridge he stopped by the railing and began staring into the water. And his sister was standing close beside him.

He had met her at the entrance to the bridge, but passed by without seeing her. Dunia had never before encountered him like this in the street, and she was struck with dismay. She stood still, not knowing whether to call out to him or not. Suddenly she saw Svidrigailov coming quickly from the direction of the Hay Market.

He seemed to be approaching cautiously. He didn't step onto the bridge but stopped on the pavement to the side, doing everything he could to keep Raskolnikov from seeing him. He had been watching Dunia for some time and had been making signs to her. She thought he was signaling to beg her not to speak to her brother but to come to him.
That was what Dunia did. She slipped past her brother and went up to Svidrigailov.

“Let's hurry away,” Svidrigailov whispered to her. “I don't want Rodion Romanovitch to know about our meeting. I should tell you I've been sitting with him in the restaurant nearby — he sought me out and I had a devil of a time getting rid of him. He has somehow heard about my letter to you and suspects something. It wasn't you who told him, of course — but if not you, then who?”
“Well, we've turned the corner now,” Dunia interrupted, “and my brother won't see us. I must tell you: I'm going no further with you. Tell me here. You can say it all in the street.”

“In the first place, I can't say it in the street; secondly, you must hear Sofya Semyonovna as well; and thirdly, I'll show you some papers… Look here — if you refuse to come with me, I'll decline to give any explanation and leave at once. But I beg you not to forget that a very curious secret of your beloved brother's rests entirely in my keeping.”
Dunia stood still, hesitating, and fixed her searching eyes on Svidrigailov.
“What are you afraid of?” he observed quietly. “The town isn't the country. And even in the country, you did me more harm than I did you.”
“Have you prepared Sofya Semyonovna?”

“No, I haven't said a word to her, and I'm not even sure she's home now. But most likely she is. She buried her stepmother today — she's not likely to be out paying visits on such a day. For the moment I don't want to speak to anyone about it, and I half regret having spoken to you. The slightest indiscretion is as good as betrayal in a matter like this. I live right there, in that house — we're coming up to it. That's the porter of our building — he knows me very well. You see, he's bowing; he sees I'm coming with a lady, and he's no doubt noticed your face already, which you'll be glad of if you're afraid of me and suspicious. Forgive me for putting it so crudely. I don't have a flat to myself; Sofya Semyonovna's room is right next to mine — she lodges in the next flat over. The whole floor is let out in lodgings. Why are you scared like a child? Am I really so terrible?”

Svidrigailov's lips twisted into a condescending smile, but he was in no mood to smile. His heart was pounding and he could scarcely breathe. He spoke rather loudly to cover his rising agitation. But Dunia didn't notice this peculiar excitement; she was too annoyed by his remark that she was frightened of him like a child and that he was so terrible to her.
“Though I know that you are not a man of honor, I am not in the least afraid of you. Lead the way,” she said with apparent composure, though her face was very pale.
Svidrigailov stopped at Sonia's room.

“Allow me to check whether she's home… She isn't. How unfortunate! But I know she may be back quite soon. If she's gone out, it can only be to see a lady about the orphans. Their mother is dead… I've been meddling and making arrangements for them. If Sofya Semyonovna doesn't come back within ten minutes, I'll send her to you — today, if you like. This is my flat. These are my two rooms. Madame Resslich, my landlady, has the next room. Now, look this way. I'll show you my chief piece of evidence: this door from my bedroom opens into two perfectly empty rooms that are up for rent. Here they are… You should look them over with some attention.”

Svidrigailov occupied two fairly large furnished rooms. Dunia was glancing around mistrustfully, but saw nothing unusual in the furniture or the arrangement of the rooms. Yet there was something to notice — for example, that Svidrigailov's flat sat exactly between two sets of almost uninhabited apartments. His rooms weren't entered directly from the corridor but through the landlady's two nearly empty rooms. Unlocking a door leading out of his bedroom, Svidrigailov showed Dunia the two empty rooms that were up for rent. Dunia stopped in the doorway, not understanding what she was meant to look at, but Svidrigailov hurried to explain.

“Look here, at this second large room. Notice that door — it's locked. Beside the door stands a chair, the only one in the two rooms. I brought it in from my own rooms so I could listen more conveniently. Just on the other side of the door is Sofya Semyonovna's table; that's where she sat talking with Rodion Romanovitch. And I sat here listening, on two consecutive evenings, for two hours each time — and of course I managed to learn something. What do you think?”
“You were listening?”
“Yes, I was. Now come back to my room — we can't sit down out here.”

He led Avdotya Romanovna back into his sitting room and offered her a chair. He sat down at the opposite side of the table, at least seven feet away from her, but probably with the same glow in his eyes that had once frightened Dunia so badly. She shuddered and again looked around distrustfully. It was an involuntary gesture; clearly she didn't want to betray her uneasiness. But the secluded position of Svidrigailov's lodging had suddenly struck her. She wanted to ask whether at least his landlady were home, but pride kept her from asking. Besides, she had another trouble in her heart, incomparably greater than fear for herself. She was in great distress.

“Here is your letter,” she said, laying it on the table. “Can what you write be true? You hint at a crime committed, you say, by my brother. You hint at it too plainly; you daren't deny it now. I must tell you: I'd heard of this stupid story before you wrote, and I don't believe a word of it. It's a disgusting and ridiculous suspicion. I know the story — and why and how it was invented. You can have no proof. You promised to prove it. Speak! But let me warn you — I don't believe you! I don't believe you!”
Dunia said all this hurriedly, and for a moment the color rushed to her face.
“If you didn't believe it, how could you have risked coming to my rooms alone? Why did you come? Simply out of curiosity?”
“Don't torment me. Speak, speak!”

“There's no denying it — you are a brave girl. Upon my word, I thought you'd have asked Mr. Razumihin to escort you here. But he wasn't with you, nor anywhere nearby. I was keeping an eye out. It's spirited of you — it proves you wanted to spare Rodion Romanovitch. But everything about you is divine… About your brother, what can I say to you? You've just seen him yourself. What did you make of him?”
“Surely that can't be the only thing you're building your case on?”

“No, not on that, but on his own words. He came here two evenings in a row to see Sofya Semyonovna. I've shown you where they sat. He made a full confession to her. He is a murderer. He killed an old woman, a pawnbroker, with whom he himself had pawned things. He killed her sister too, a peddler woman called Lizaveta, who happened to come in while he was murdering her sister. He killed them with an axe he had brought with him. He murdered them in order to rob them, and rob them he did. He took money and various items… He told all of this, word for word, to Sofya Semyonovna — the only person who knows his secret. But she has had no part in the murder, by word or deed; she was as horrified by it as you are now. Don't worry, she won't betray him.”
“It cannot be,” Dunia muttered, her lips white. She gasped for breath. “It cannot be. There was not the slightest cause, no sort of reason… It's a lie, a lie!”

“He robbed her — that was the cause. He took money and things. It's true that by his own admission he made no use of the money or the things, but hid them under a stone, where they still are. But that was because he didn't dare make use of them.”
“But how could he steal, how could he rob? How could he even dream of it?” Dunia cried, jumping up from the chair. “You know him, you've seen him — can he be a thief?”
She seemed to be pleading with Svidrigailov; she had completely forgotten her fear.

“There are thousands and millions of combinations and possibilities, Avdotya Romanovna. A thief steals and knows he's a scoundrel, but I've heard of a gentleman who broke open the mail. Who knows — very likely he thought he was doing a gentlemanly thing! Of course I wouldn't have believed it myself if I'd been told of it the way you're being told now, but I believe my own ears. He explained all the reasons for it to Sofya Semyonovna too. At first she didn't believe her ears, but in the end she believed her own eyes.”
“What… were the reasons?”

“It's a long story, Avdotya Romanovna. Here's… how shall I put it? — a theory of a sort, the same one by which I, for instance, hold that a single misdeed is permissible if the principal aim is good — a solitary wrongdoing and hundreds of good deeds! It's galling too, of course, for a gifted young man of overweening pride to know that if he only had, say, a paltry three thousand, his whole career and his whole future would take a different shape — and yet not to have that three thousand. Add to that the nervous irritation of hunger, of living in a hole, of wearing rags, of a vivid sense of his own social position and that of his sister and mother. Above all, vanity — pride and vanity — though God knows he may have good qualities too… I'm not blaming him, please don't think that; besides, it's none of my business. A special little theory got mixed up in it too — a theory of a sort — dividing humanity, you see, into the ordinary and the superior, meaning persons to whom the law does not apply because of their superiority, persons who make the laws for the rest of mankind — the ordinary, that is. It's fine as a theory, une théorie comme une autre. Napoleon attracted him enormously — that is, what affected him was that so many men of genius have had no hesitation about wrongdoing, have stepped over the law without a second thought. He seems to have imagined that he was a genius too — that is, he was convinced of it for a time. He has suffered a great deal and is still suffering from the idea that he could formulate a theory, but was incapable of boldly stepping over the law — and so he is not a man of genius. And that's humiliating for any proud young man, especially in our day…”
“But remorse? You deny him any moral feeling, then? Is that what he's like?”

“Ah, Avdotya Romanovna, everything is in a muddle now — not that it was ever in particularly good order. Russians in general are broad in their ideas, Avdotya Romanovna, broad like their land and exceedingly inclined toward the fantastic, the chaotic. But it's a misfortune to be broad without a special genius. Do you remember what a lot of talk we had together on this very subject, sitting on the terrace in the evenings after supper? You even used to reproach me with breadth! Who knows — perhaps we were talking at the very time when he was lying here thinking over his plan. We have no sacred traditions in our country, especially in the educated class, Avdotya Romanovna. At best someone will cobble them together out of books or some old chronicle. But those are mostly the scholars and old-fashioned fellows, so much so that it would be almost ill-bred in a man of society. You know my opinions in general, anyway. I blame no one. I do nothing at all, and I persist in that. But we've talked of this more than once before. I was even so happy as to interest you in my opinions… You are very pale, Avdotya Romanovna.”
“I know his theory. I read that article of his about men to whom everything is permitted. Razumihin brought it to me.”
“Mr. Razumihin? Your brother's article? In a magazine? Is there such an article? I didn't know. It must be interesting. But where are you going, Avdotya Romanovna?”
“I want to see Sofya Semyonovna,” Dunia said faintly. “How do I get to her? Perhaps she's come back. I must see her at once. Perhaps she…”
Avdotya Romanovna couldn't finish. Her breath literally failed her.
“Sofya Semyonovna won't be back until night — at least, I don't think she will. She was supposed to be back right away, but if not, then she won't be in until quite late.”
“Ah, then you're lying! I see it now… you were lying… lying all the time… I don't believe you! I don't believe you!” Dunia cried, completely losing her head.
Almost fainting, she sank onto a chair that Svidrigailov hastened to offer her.
“Avdotya Romanovna, what is it? Control yourself! Here is some water. Take a little…”
He sprinkled some water on her. Dunia shuddered and came to herself.

“It has acted violently,” Svidrigailov muttered to himself, frowning. “Avdotya Romanovna, calm yourself! Believe me, he has friends. We'll save him. Would you like me to take him abroad? I have money, I can get a ticket in three days. And as for the murder — he'll yet do all sorts of good deeds to atone for it. Calm yourself. He may become a great man yet. Well, how are you? How do you feel?”
“Cruel man! To be able to mock it! Let me go…”
“Where are you going?”
“To him. Where is he? Do you know? Why is this door locked? We came in through that door, and now it's locked. When did you manage to lock it?”

“We can't exactly be shouting about this all over the flat. I'm not mocking — it's simply that I'm sick of talking like this. But how can you go in such a state? Do you want to betray him? You'll drive him into a fury, and he'll turn himself in. Let me tell you — he is already being watched; they're already on his trail. You'll simply be handing him over. Wait a little: I saw him and was talking to him just now. He can still be saved. Wait a moment, sit down. Let us think it over together. I asked you to come in order to discuss this alone with you and to consider it properly. Please, sit down!”
“How can you save him? Can he really be saved?”
Dunia sat down. Svidrigailov sat down beside her.
“It all depends on you, on you, on you alone,” he began, his eyes glowing, almost in a whisper, barely able to get the words out for emotion.
Dunia drew back from him in alarm. He too was trembling all over.

“You… one word from you, and he is saved. I… I will save him. I have money and friends. I'll send him away at once. I'll get a passport — two passports, one for him and one for me. I have friends… capable people… If you like, I'll get a passport for you… for your mother… What do you want with Razumihin? I love you too… I love you beyond everything… Let me kiss the hem of your dress, let me, let me… The very rustle of it is too much for me. Tell me, ‘Do that,' and I'll do it. I'll do everything. I'll do the impossible. Whatever you believe, I'll believe. I'll do anything — anything! Don't, don't look at me that way. Do you realize you are killing me?…”
He was nearly starting to rave… Something seemed to rush to his head all at once. Dunia jumped up and rushed to the door.
“Open it! Open it!” she called, shaking the door. “Open it! Is there no one out there?”
Svidrigailov got up and came back to himself. His still-trembling lips slowly broke into an angry, mocking smile.
“There is no one at home,” he said quietly and emphatically. “The landlady has gone out, and it's a waste of time to shout like that. You're only exciting yourself for nothing.”
“Where is the key? Open the door at once, at once, you vile man!”
“I've lost the key and can't find it.”
“This is an outrage!” Dunia cried, turning pale as death. She rushed to the farthest corner, where she hurriedly barricaded herself with a little table.
She didn't scream, but she fixed her eyes on her tormentor and watched every movement he made.
Svidrigailov remained standing at the other end of the room, facing her. He was outwardly composed, at least in appearance, but his face was pale as before. The mocking smile did not leave his face.

“You spoke of outrage just now, Avdotya Romanovna. In that case, you can be sure I've taken my precautions. Sofya Semyonovna is not at home. The Kapernaumovs are far away — there are five locked rooms between us. I am at least twice as strong as you are, and I have nothing else to fear either. Because you couldn't complain afterwards. You surely wouldn't really be willing to betray your brother? Besides, no one would believe you. Why would a girl have come alone to visit a solitary man at his lodgings? So that even if you did sacrifice your brother, you could prove nothing. It's very difficult to prove an assault, Avdotya Romanovna.”
“Scoundrel!” Dunia whispered in outrage.

“As you like, but do notice I was only speaking by way of a general proposition. My personal conviction is that you're entirely right — violence is hateful. I only said that to show you that you need feel no remorse even if… you were willing to save your brother of your own free will, as I'm suggesting. You would simply be submitting to circumstances — to violence, in fact, if we must use that word. Think it over. Your brother's fate and your mother's are in your hands. I will be your slave… for the rest of my life… I'll wait right here.”

Svidrigailov sat down on the sofa about eight steps from Dunia. She no longer had the slightest doubt of his unyielding determination. Besides, she knew him. Suddenly she pulled a revolver out of her pocket, cocked it, and laid it in her hand on the table. Svidrigailov jumped up.

“Aha! So that's it, is it?” he cried, surprised but smiling maliciously. “Well, that completely changes the look of things. You've made things wonderfully easier for me, Avdotya Romanovna. But where did you get the revolver? Was it Mr. Razumihin? Why, it's my revolver, an old friend! And how I've hunted for it! The shooting lessons I gave you out in the country have not been wasted.”

“It's not your revolver — it belonged to Marfa Petrovna, whom you killed, wretch! There was nothing of yours in her house. I took it when I began to suspect what you were capable of. If you dare take one step forward, I swear I'll kill you.” She was frantic.
“But your brother? I ask out of curiosity,” said Svidrigailov, still standing where he was.
“Inform on him if you want! Don't move! Don't come any closer! I'll shoot! You poisoned your wife — I know; you are a murderer yourself!” She held the revolver ready.
“Are you so certain I poisoned Marfa Petrovna?”
“You did! You hinted at it yourself; you talked to me about poison… I know you went to get some… you had it ready… It was your doing… It must have been your doing… Scoundrel!”
“Even if that were true, it would have been for your sake… you would have been the cause.”
“You are lying! I have always hated you, always…”

“Oho, Avdotya Romanovna! You seem to have forgotten how you softened toward me in the heat of your reforming zeal. I saw it in your eyes. Do you remember that moonlit night, when the nightingale was singing?”
“That's a lie,” said Dunia, her eyes flashing with fury, “that's a lie and a slander!”
“A lie? Well, if you like, it's a lie. I made it up. Women ought not to be reminded of such things,” he smiled. “I know you'll shoot, you pretty wild creature. Well — shoot away!”

Dunia raised the revolver and, deathly pale, stared at him, measuring the distance and waiting for his first movement. Her lower lip was white and quivering, and her big black eyes flashed like fire. He had never seen her so handsome. The fire glowing in her eyes at the moment she raised the revolver seemed to kindle him, and there was a pang of anguish in his heart. He took a step forward, and a shot rang out. The bullet grazed his hair and flew into the wall behind. He stood still and laughed softly.

“The wasp has stung me. She aimed straight at my head. What's this? Blood?” He pulled out his handkerchief to wipe away the blood, which was running in a thin stream down his right temple. The bullet seemed to have just grazed the skin.
Dunia lowered the revolver and looked at Svidrigailov not so much in terror as in a kind of wild amazement. She seemed not to understand what she was doing or what was happening.
“Well, you missed! Fire again, I'll wait,” Svidrigailov said softly, still smiling, but grimly now. “If you go on like that, I'll have time to grab you before you can cock it again.”
Dunia started, quickly cocked the pistol, and raised it once more.
“Let me be!” she cried in despair. “I swear I'll shoot again. I… I'll kill you.”
“Well… at three paces you can hardly help it. But if you don't… then.” His eyes flashed and he took two steps forward. Dunia pulled the trigger again — it misfired.
“You haven't loaded it properly. Never mind — you still have another charge. Get it ready, I'll wait.”

He stood facing her, two paces away, waiting and gazing at her with wild determination, with feverishly passionate, stubborn, fixed eyes. Dunia saw that he would sooner die than let her go. “And… now, of course, she would kill him, at two paces!” Suddenly she flung the revolver aside.

“She's dropped it!” said Svidrigailov in surprise, and drew a deep breath. A weight seemed to have rolled off his heart — perhaps not only the fear of death; indeed, he may hardly have felt that in the moment. It was deliverance from another feeling, darker and more bitter, which he himself could not have defined.

He went up to Dunia and gently put his arm around her waist. She did not resist, but, trembling like a leaf, looked at him with pleading eyes. He tried to say something, but his lips moved without being able to form a sound.
“Let me go,” Dunia implored. Svidrigailov shuddered. Her voice now was quite different.
“Then you don't love me?” he asked softly. Dunia shook her head.
“And… and you can't? Never?” he whispered in despair.
“Never!”

There followed a moment of terrible, silent struggle in Svidrigailov's heart. He looked at her with an indescribable gaze. Suddenly he withdrew his arm, turned quickly to the window, and stood facing it. Another moment passed.
“Here is the key.”
He took it out of the left pocket of his coat and laid it on the table behind him, without turning or looking at Dunia.
“Take it! Hurry!”
He stared stubbornly out of the window. Dunia went up to the table to take the key.
“Hurry! Hurry!” repeated Svidrigailov, still without turning or moving. But there seemed to be a terrible significance in the tone of that “hurry.”

Dunia understood it, snatched up the key, flew to the door, unlocked it quickly, and rushed out of the room. A minute later, beside herself, she was running along the canal bank in the direction of X. Bridge.

Svidrigailov stood at the window for three minutes. At last he slowly turned, looked around him, and passed his hand across his forehead. A strange smile contorted his face — a pitiful, sad, weak smile, a smile of despair. The blood, already drying, smeared his hand. He looked at it angrily, then dampened a towel and washed his temple. The revolver Dunia had flung away was lying near the door, and it suddenly caught his eye. He picked it up and examined it. It was a little pocket three-barrel revolver of old-fashioned construction. There were still two charges and one cap left in it. It could be fired again. He thought for a moment, put the revolver in his pocket, took his hat, and went out.
